pedagogy.summary: Likelihood language gives children words — impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain — to describe how probable everyday events are, before any numbers. The teaching aim is correct USE in context: mapping each word onto the composition of a situation (how many of each outcome), and reserving 'certain'/'impossible' for the true endpoints while using the graded middle for everything else. It is the gateway to the 0-to-1 scale and to comparing likelihoods.
bestPractices: Anchor a physical 'likelihood line' (a washing line / strip labelled impossible → even chance → certain) and have children peg real events onto it, justifying placements aloud

Start from everyday, personally-meaningful events ('it will get dark tonight', 'it will snow in July') then move to structured chance devices (bags of counters, spinners) where the composition can be inspected
Deliberately contrast 'likely' with 'certain' and 'unlikely' with 'impossible' using a mostly-red bag: red is likely but a blue draw is still possible, so red is not certain
Insist children give a reason grounded in the numbers ('most of them are red') rather than personal desire ('I want red')
Use unequal situations early (7 red, 3 blue; a spinner with one big section) so 'even chance' is not over-generalised to any two-outcome case
keyRepresentations: Likelihood line / probability word-scale strip (impossible ↔ certain)
Bags of coloured counters with visible, countable composition
Spinners with equal vs unequal sections
Everyday-event cards to sort and order
commonMisconceptions: Treating 'even chance' as meaning 'any situation with two possible outcomes' (e.g. calling a 1-red / 5-blue draw 'even chance' because there are two colours)
Collapsing the graded words to guarantees — 'likely' taken to mean it will definitely happen, 'unlikely' that it definitely won't
Confusing 'impossible' (cannot happen, probability 0) with 'very unlikely' (rare but possible) — e.g. calling a rare draw 'impossible'
Judging likelihood by personal preference or wishful thinking rather than by how many of each outcome there are

learn.summary: Likelihood Language (ages 9-10, Mathematics/Probability): children learn to USE and justify the words impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain to describe how probable everyday events and chance-device outcomes are, before any numbers. The teaching aim is correct use in context — mapping each word onto the composition of a situation (how many of each outcome), reserving 'certain'/'impossible' for the true endpoints and using the graded middle for everything else. This is the gateway to the 0-to-1 scale and to comparing likelihoods. Core activity is open dialogue where the child generates and repairs their own wording against outcomes that push back; a live likelihood line/strip and sorting tasks are strong supports, and a tap-to-reveal reference scene can accompany them.

activities.title: The Chance-master's bag: say it, then watch it happen
feedback: If the child says 'red is certain', take out and show a blue counter (pick one deliberately, or keep drawing until one comes out, since a single random draw is usually red): 'Certain? But look, here is a blue I could pull. So is red certain, or only likely?' — let the over-strong word fail against a real possible outcome.

If the child says 'even chance' because there are two colours, count together: '7 red vs 3 blue is not equal, so it is not an even chance — what would the bag need for red and blue to be an even chance?' (equal numbers).
If the child accepts '7 on a 1–6 die is very unlikely', ask 'could it EVER come up? Which faces are on the die?' — since there is no 7, it cannot happen, so it is impossible, not merely rare.
If the child calls a green draw 'very unlikely', ask 'could it EVER happen? Show me a green counter.' There is none, so it is impossible, not merely rare.
If the child treats blue (unlikely) as 'impossible', point out some blue counters are present, so it can still happen — contrast 'rarely' with 'never'.
Affirm reasons grounded in counts ('most are red, so likely') and press on reasons grounded in desire ('I want red') by asking what the counters show.
activities.rationale: This is a LANGUAGE objective whose mastery is producing and justifying the words in context, so an open, unscripted dialogue that makes the child generate (not select) the vocabulary and repair it against real outcomes is intended to target the objective directly. Using unequal compositions guards against over-generalising 'even chance'; drawing the rare outcome and probing the impossible endpoint confront the guarantee and impossible-vs-unlikely misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Likelihood words (certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible) map onto the 0-to-1 scale, and a key misconception is treating any two-outcome situation as an even chance — a cube with 1 red and 5 blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not even.

Even young children can register that the more numerous of two outcomes is more likely (additive 'more/less' reasoning), and the equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes are equally likely — is a documented misconception in children's probabilistic reasoning.
learnerActions: Look into a bag you can see holds mostly red counters (e.g. 7 red and 3 blue) with the composition visible.
Before any draw, say in words how likely a red draw is and WHY, grounding the reason in the numbers ('most of them are red') rather than wanting red.

When you declare red 'certain', watch the game-master take out and show a blue counter (picked on purpose, or by drawing until one appears, because a single random draw will usually be red), then repair your word: was red certain, or only likely? Explain the difference.

Answer the opposite trap: the game-master suggests 'landing on 7 with this ordinary 1–6 die is only very unlikely, isn't it?' — decide whether 7 is very unlikely (rare but possible) or impossible (cannot happen at all), and say why.
Describe a green draw ('there are no green counters'), and a 'red or blue' draw ('only those two colours exist'), choosing and justifying a word for each.
Reject vague answers: if you say '50-50', be ready for 'but there are 7 red and 3 blue — is that even?' and recount to decide.
activities.intendedInsight: Each likelihood word corresponds to how many of each outcome there are; 'likely' is not a guarantee and 'impossible' (cannot happen at all) is stronger than 'very unlikely' (rare but possible). 'Even chance' requires equal numbers, not merely two possible outcomes.

activities.title: Physical likelihood line: peg real events and justify
feedback: If every event lands at the extremes or at 'even chance', ask for a reason tied to counts or frequency, and nudge toward the graded middle only for events that are not truly all-or-none or equally balanced.
If an unequal spinner/bag is called 'even chance', compare the total size or count for the outcome against the total for everything else: if those two totals are unequal, it cannot be an even chance.
Praise placements justified by 'most/few/none' rather than by what the child hopes happens.
activities.rationale: Anchoring a physical scale and pegging real events makes the ordering concrete and the reasoning public; starting from everyday events before structured devices connects the words to meaning, and insisting on number-grounded reasons addresses wishful-thinking and equiprobability errors.
sourceClaims: Even young children can register that the more numerous of two outcomes is more likely (additive 'more/less' reasoning), and the equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes are equally likely — is a documented misconception in children's probabilistic reasoning.
learnerActions: Set up a washing line or paper strip labelled impossible → unlikely → even chance → likely → certain.

Peg everyday, personally-meaningful events onto it, saying your placement aloud: 'it will get dark tonight', 'it will snow in July', 'I'll flip heads', 'the sun will rise tomorrow' (for the weather and daylight events, think about where you live: snow in July is likely in some southern places, and near the poles there are times with no sunset or no sunrise).
Move to structured chance devices where composition is inspectable — bags of counters, spinners with equal and unequal sections — and peg outcomes from those.
Place at least one deliberately unequal situation (7 red/3 blue; a spinner with one big section) and justify why it is NOT an even chance.
Say out loud the reason for each placement, referring to how many of each outcome there are.
activities.intendedInsight: Events can be ordered along a graded scale from impossible to certain, and placement is decided by composition, not by preference — unequal situations sit away from 'even chance'.

activities.title: Live likelihood strip with an adjustable bag
feedback: If the child relies on the suggested-word zone without reasoning, cover it and ask them to predict the word before revealing.
When blue counters are removed, prompt: 'has red become certain yet? Is there still any blue left?' to tie 'certain' to zero alternatives.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable strip makes the mapping from composition to word felt and correctable in real time, while still requiring the child to produce the word. The recolouring/slider and suggested-word zone are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.
sourceClaims: Likelihood words (certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible) map onto the 0-to-1 scale, and a key misconception is treating any two-outcome situation as an even chance — a cube with 1 red and 5 blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not even.
learnerActions: Drop an event card onto a 0-to-1 likelihood strip and SAY the word that fits before confirming.
Change the number of red vs blue counters (e.g. with a slider) and watch which word best fits shift as the composition changes.
Remove the blue counters one at a time and predict, then say, which word changes and why ('likely' sliding toward 'certain' as blue is removed).
Always voice the word yourself rather than only reading the suggested-word zone.
activities.intendedInsight: The word that fits a situation depends on and moves with the composition; as favourable outcomes dominate, the likelihood slides toward 'certain', and only when none of the other outcome remains is it 'certain' (and the absent outcome 'impossible').

activities.title: Sort and order events (recognition check)
feedback: If the child accepts '1-vs-5 as even chance', have them count and compare: two colours is not enough; the counts must be equal.
If sorting is correct but reasons are missing, ask 'why does this one go here?' and require a count-based justification, since a correct label alone does not show the reasoning behind it.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and sequencing test recognition of the words and can surface misconceptions through targeted distractors, but selecting from options checks recognition rather than the child's own justified use; pairing each placement with a spoken reason partly bridges this gap.
sourceClaims: Likelihood words (certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible) map onto the 0-to-1 scale, and a key misconception is treating any two-outcome situation as an even chance — a cube with 1 red and 5 blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not even.
learnerActions: Sort event cards into five groups: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain.
Order a set of events along the scale from least to most likely.
Judge deliberately tricky distractors, e.g. a two-colour but 1-vs-5 draw offered as 'even chance', and decide whether the label is right.
For each card you place, add a spoken or written reason comparing how many of each outcome there are.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising which word fits is a useful step, but the real target is correct, justified use — distractors built from common misconceptions reveal whether the word is being applied for the right reason.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal reference scene (worked examples)
feedback: Encourage self-prediction before revealing so the scene supports, rather than replaces, the child's own wording.
Point out that each revealed reason refers to how many of each outcome there are — the same justification the child should give.
activities.rationale: A static tap-to-reveal scene can present the vocabulary and worked reasons clearly, but being pre-baked it does not by itself elicit the child producing or comparing language; it works best as a reference alongside the dialogue or physical line, not as the sole activity.
learnerActions: Browse events arranged along a likelihood line and tap each to reveal the correct word and the numeric reason behind it.
Use this as a reference or worked-example companion when checking your own reasoning after attempting an event yourself.
Try to name the word yourself first, then tap to compare with the revealed answer and reason.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing worked reasons (why red is likely but not certain, why green is impossible) models the count-based justification expected of the child's own answers.

constraints: The objective is correct USE and justification of the five words in context; activities must make the child produce and justify the vocabulary, not merely select it.
Justifications must be grounded in the composition (how many of each outcome), not in personal preference or wishful thinking.

Reserve 'certain' and 'impossible' for the true endpoints (all favourable / zero favourable) and use the graded middle for everything else; do not let 'likely' become a guarantee or 'unlikely' become 'impossible'.

Keep 'impossible' (cannot happen at all, e.g. 7 on a 1–6 die or a green draw when none are present) distinct from 'very unlikely' (rare but possible); never present a strictly impossible outcome as a graded-middle case.

Use unequal compositions early (e.g. 7 red/3 blue, a spinner with one big section) so 'even chance' is not over-generalised to any two-outcome case; when comparing two represented outcomes, 'even chance' requires equal numbers.

Sorting/sequencing and the tap-to-reveal scene are recognition or reference scaffolds: they can assess classification or model reasoning but do not on their own elicit the child's independent, justified use of the words — pair them with spoken/written reasons or follow with open dialogue.
The live strip's slider/recolouring and suggested-word zone are optional illustrative interactions, not required mechanisms; the child must still voice the word themselves.

A spatial/3D environment is not required for this vocabulary-focused objective, which centres on producing and justifying words rather than spatial reasoning; the source judged it to add little over a flat scale and dialogue, but treat this as a scoped, untested design judgement, not a universal claim that 3D media add nothing.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Self-audit of worked examples: for a visible 7 red / 3 blue bag — red draw = likely (most but not all), blue = unlikely (few but present), green = impossible (none), red-or-blue = certain (only those two colours). These are internally consistent. 'Even chance' for red vs blue would require equal counts (e.g. 5 red / 5 blue); the 7/3 and 1/5 cases are correctly flagged as NOT even chance.

The 'die lands on 7' example is used to contrast impossible vs very-unlikely; landing on 7 on a standard 1–6 die is strictly impossible (cannot happen), so the dialogue has the character offer the under-strong 'very unlikely' for the child to correct to 'impossible'. The original source phrasing ('the die can land on 7 — very unlikely?') is preserved in intent but reframed so the prompt does not pre-answer it.

The source's judgement that a 3D environment adds little conceptual leverage here has been softened to a scoped, untested design judgement per guidance; it should not be read as a universal claim that 3D media add nothing.
No arithmetic, fractions, or force/motion content requiring further correction was identified in this row.

probeDeeper: You said red is likely — is it certain? Could you ever pull out a blue instead?
Why is that not an 'even chance'? What would the bag have to look like for red and blue to be an even chance?
Is 'impossible' the same as 'very unlikely'? Give me one event that is impossible and one that is only very unlikely.
If I took out all the blue counters, which word would change, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correct USE: 'red' = likely (most but not all are red), 'blue' = unlikely (some but few), 'green' = impossible (there are none), 'red or blue' = certain (only those two colours exist). Justifications should refer to how many of each colour there are, and the strip should order them impossible(green) → unlikely(blue) → likely(red) → certain(red-or-blue).

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'even chance' for any situation with two outcomes ('it's 50-50, there's red and blue') regardless of how many of each there are
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront directly: count them together — 7 red vs 3 blue is not equal, so it is not an even chance; ask what the bag would need for 'even chance' to be true (equal numbers)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the 7-red/3-blue draw 'even chance' or '50-50' because two colours are present, without comparing the counts

errorPatterns.pattern: Collapses graded words into guarantees — 'likely' means it will happen, 'unlikely' means it won't
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the rare blue in front of them to show likely is not certain and unlikely is not impossible; contrast 'most of the time' with 'always/never'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a red draw is 'certain' or 'will happen' because most are red, and treats blue as effectively impossible

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses 'impossible' (cannot happen, 0) with 'very unlikely' (rare but possible)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'could it EVER happen?' to separate the endpoints (impossible/certain) from the graded middle (how often); show there is no green counter at all, so it truly cannot happen
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the green draw 'very unlikely' rather than impossible, or calls a rare-but-present outcome 'impossible'

responseLevels.gap: Uses only 'maybe / will / won't' or blanket '50-50' for everything; no graded vocabulary; treats any two-outcome situation as even chance
responseLevels.full: Uses all five words correctly across varied events AND justifies each by comparing favourable to total outcomes (red is likely-not-certain because most but not all are red), and cleanly distinguishes impossible from very-unlikely
responseLevels.partial: Uses the five words but unreliably in the middle — conflates likely with certain or impossible with very-unlikely; can label single events but justifies by preference or by naming colours rather than comparing how many of each

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put in front of the child a bag holding 7 red and 3 blue counters (composition visible), and read out four events: 'I pull out a red', 'I pull out a blue', 'I pull out a green', 'I pull out a red or a blue'. Ask them to describe each using probability words — certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible — and to say WHY for each. Then ask them to place the four events on a strip from impossible to certain. Listen for the words used correctly and justified by the composition; do not offer options or expect a number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child mapping words to composition calls red 'likely' (not certain, because a blue is still possible), blue 'unlikely', green 'impossible' (zero in the bag), and red-or-blue 'certain'. A child reasoning from surface features says 'even chance' for red-vs-blue because there are two colours, calls blue 'impossible' (confusing rare with can't-happen), or calls red 'certain' (likely taken as a guarantee). The justification, not the label, reveals which.
